reason: The glucose-rich blood and pancreatic sensing cells suggest a way to start the after-meal response, though I don't yet know exactly what the cells will do.
expectation: The pancreatic cells will respond to the glucose in the blood.

effect: The glucose first had to be added to the body; the pancreatic sensing cells may now respond to the rising blood glucose.
reaction: I was surprised that the blood had to be connected to the body before the sensing cells could be used.
reason: The picture places pancreatic sensing cells beside blood vessels, so they seem suited to detect the body's rising glucose.
expectation: The pancreatic cells will sense the rise and start an after-meal response.

effect: The pancreatic beta cells released insulin into the blood, with routes marked toward muscle and liver.
reaction: The picture makes the pancreas-to-blood signal clearer.
reason: The insulin route points toward muscle, and skeletal muscle is available to try.
expectation: The muscle will respond to insulin and take up some glucose from the blood.

effect: Insulin helped muscle take up glucose, and the goal now shifts to keeping glucose available between meals.
reaction: The later inset clearly showed the response easing as blood glucose fell.
reason: The clock shows glucose continuing to be used while food supplies less, so advancing time should start the between-meals response.

choice.combine: Body taking up glucose into muscle

expectation: Blood glucose will decrease as time passes between meals, prompting a response.

effect: Blood glucose has fallen between meals, while glycogen remains in the liver.
reaction: The clock and blood inset make the change easy to follow.
reason: The pancreatic sensing cells include alpha cells as well as the beta cells that responded earlier; I can try them for the falling-glucose response, although I don't yet know what they release.
expectation: The pancreatic cells will respond to falling blood glucose and start a signal to keep glucose available.

alternatives.reason: The liver could release stored glucose, as it did earlier, but a sensing step may come first.

effect: Falling glucose led the pancreatic alpha cells to release glucagon, with its route pointing toward the liver.
reaction: The contrast with the earlier insulin response is clear.
reason: The glucagon route points to the liver, and earlier the liver released glucose from stored glycogen.
expectation: The liver will respond to glucagon by releasing glucose from its glycogen stores into the blood.

effect: The liver broke down glycogen and released glucose into the blood; as glucose rose, glucagon release decreased. Both goals are complete.
reaction: The sequence made the between-meals feedback easier to follow.

mostWorthwhile.text: Following the insulin and glucagon responses was worthwhile because the same body responded differently after a meal and between meals.

leastWorthwhile.text: Adding the glucose-rich blood to the body first felt like an extra setup step; I initially expected the sensing cells to respond directly.

surprise.text: I was surprised that falling glucose prompted different pancreatic cells to release glucagon, and that the signal eased as glucose rose again.

arbitrary.text: The need to connect the glucose-rich blood to the body before using the sensing cells was not obvious to me, though the result clarified it.

continue.text: I would choose to continue: seeing the two responses connect to earlier liver and muscle discoveries made me curious about how other systems work together.
